title: Own scratch files and verify parser sources before importing
environment: A Python command-line diagnostic dynamically imports a parser from a local source tree and writes a result into a directory that concurrent runs may share.
goal: Prevent scratch-file collisions, cleanup of another run's file, and importing parser files whose expected source hashes do not match.
approach: A fixed temporary filename was derived from the requested output path. The script checked whether that path existed, wrote to it, and removed it during cleanup. A parser was imported from a caller-supplied local directory, while source hashes were recorded after execution. The verifier was changed to create a unique file exclusively in the destination directory, retain its filesystem identity, and check that identity immediately before cleanup. It hashes expected parser sources and compares them with pinned values before importing the parser, and disables Python bytecode writes before the dynamic import.
what_worked: An offline synthetic diagnostic exited successfully. Controls confirmed that a preexisting path was preserved, overlapping calls received distinct scratch paths, failure cleanup removed the owned scratch file, a replacement inode survived cleanup, and a mismatched parser source hash was rejected before import. The result recorded pre-import hash checks and disabled bytecode writes. The application-level conclusion remained unproven, with no mapping asserted.
what_failed: The fixed scratch-path design could race under overlapping calls, truncate a file created by another process, or remove a path it did not own. Recording hashes only after execution did not establish which parser source files had been checked before import. A dangling-symlink cleanup control could not be performed because the operating system denied that operation.
why: Existence checks and later writes are separate operations, so concurrent processes can race between them. Unconditional cleanup treats a shared pathname as ownership proof. Post-execution hashes are retrospective evidence and do not verify source files before import. Dynamic imports may also create bytecode cache files unless bytecode generation is disabled.
improved_method: Create an exclusive random scratch file in the target directory, record its filesystem identity immediately, and check that identity immediately before cleanup. Compute and validate expected source hashes before importing code. Disable bytecode generation before the import. Run controls for preexisting paths, concurrent calls, controlled failures, path replacement, and source mismatch. Report OS-denied controls as skipped rather than passed. Keep the application conclusion unproven unless separate semantic evidence supports it.
when_to_use: Diagnostics or tools that share an output directory, create temporary files, dynamically import code from a local tree, or claim to check a specific source revision before importing.
when_not_to_use: This pattern alone does not provide atomic protection against a hostile change between the path identity check and unlink, and it does not establish application-level semantics. Use stronger operating-system primitives or a private isolated directory when the threat model requires them.
known_limitations: The identity check followed by unlink is not atomic, leaving a time-of-check/time-of-use window. The pre-import hash check does not make source bytes immutable between hashing and loading or invalidate already-cached modules. Cached-module behavior was not tested in this fresh command-line run. The dangling-symlink control was skipped after an operating-system permission denial. The controls were synthetic and do not establish general application correctness.
